source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 7 (PDF 139-173, printed 136-170); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 7 (Waves and Vibrations), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 A wave is a regular disturbance that carries:

options.text: only the particles of the medium

blocks.explanation: A wave is a regular disturbance or variation that carries energy, which spreads out from the source (7.1).

book_ref.quote: A wave is a regular disturbance or variation that carries energy

blocks.prompt: 2 When a stone is thrown into a pond, the water particles:

options.text: move up and down at their own places

blocks.explanation: The water particles move up and down at their own places, creating a repeating pattern that spreads out (7.1).

book_ref.quote: The water particles move up and down at their own places

blocks.prompt: 3 The displacement of a particle of a wave is its distance in a specified direction from its:
blocks.explanation: Displacement is the distance in a specified direction from the rest / equilibrium position (7.1).

book_ref.quote: The displacement of a particle of a wave is its distance in a specified direction

blocks.prompt: 4 In the waveform of Fig. 7.2, displacement is plotted on the y-axis and the x-axis shows:

options.text: distance in the direction of energy travel

blocks.explanation: The x-axis of the waveform is the distance in the direction of energy travel, as Fig. 7.2 labels it (7.1, book correction).

book_ref.quote: The x-axis of this waveform is the distance in the direction of energy travel

blocks.prompt: 5 The maximum displacement of the particles of the medium from the equilibrium position is called:
blocks.explanation: Amplitude (A) is the maximum displacement of the wave (or particles) from its equilibrium position (7.1).

book_ref.quote: Amplitude (A): The maximum displacement of the wave

blocks.prompt: 6 The distance between two consecutive similar points on a wave that are in phase is the:
blocks.explanation: Wavelength (λ) is the distance between two consecutive similar points on the wave that are in phase (7.1).

book_ref.quote: Wavelength (λ): The distance between two consecutive similar points

blocks.prompt: 7 The number of oscillations or cycles per second of a wave is its:
blocks.explanation: Frequency (f) is the number of oscillations/vibrations or cycles per second (7.1).

book_ref.quote: The number of oscillations/vibrations or cycles per second.

blocks.prompt: 8 A wave has a frequency of 250 Hz. Its period is:
blocks.explanation: T = 1/f = 1/250 = 0.004 s; period is the reciprocal of frequency (7.1).

book_ref.quote: it is the reciprocal of the frequency T = 1/f

blocks.prompt: 9 In obtaining v = fλ from v = λ/T, the step used is:
blocks.explanation: Speed = distance/time = λ/T; since 1/T = f, v = fλ (Eq. 7.1).

book_ref.quote: If a wave crest moves one wavelength λ in one period of oscillation T

blocks.prompt: 10 A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz has a wavelength of 0.68 m. Its speed is:

book_ref.quote: 5. Speed (v): The speed at which the wave travels.

blocks.prompt: 11 The relative position of a point on the wave at a given time is called its:
blocks.explanation: Phase (θ) is the relative position of a point on the wave at a given time (7.1).

book_ref.quote: 6. Phase (θ): The relative position of a point on the wave at a given time.

blocks.prompt: 12 In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium vibrate:

options.text: along the direction of energy travel
opposite to the direction of energy travel only
at right angle to the direction of energy travel

blocks.explanation: In a transverse wave the vibrations of the particles are at right angle to the direction in which the energy travels.

book_ref.quote: A transverse wave is one in which the vibrations of the particles are at right angle

blocks.prompt: 13 A wave in which the particles vibrate along (parallel to) the direction of energy travel is a:
blocks.explanation: In a longitudinal wave the vibration of the particles is along or parallel to the direction of energy travel.

book_ref.quote: the direction of the vibration of the particles is along or parallel to

blocks.prompt: 14 Waves that require a physical medium (solid, liquid or gas) to propagate are:
blocks.explanation: Mechanical waves require a physical medium; examples are water waves, sound waves and seismic waves.

book_ref.quote: These waves require a physical medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to propagate.

blocks.prompt: 15 Which of the following can travel through vacuum?
blocks.explanation: X-rays are electromagnetic waves, which do not require a medium and can travel through vacuum; the others are mechanical.

book_ref.quote: They do not require a medium to propagate and therefore, can travel through vacuum.

blocks.prompt: 16 Electron waves in atoms (de-Broglie waves) are an example of:
blocks.explanation: Quantum waves are associated with particles like electrons and photons, e.g. matter waves or de-Broglie waves.

book_ref.quote: Quantum waves are associated with particles like electrons and photons.

blocks.prompt: 17 Waves that propagate along the interface between two mediums are called:
blocks.explanation: Surface waves propagate along surfaces or interfaces between two mediums, e.g. wind-driven ocean surface waves.

book_ref.quote: Surface waves propagate along surfaces or interfaces between two mediums.

blocks.prompt: 18 The energy of the Sun reaches the Earth through empty space because light waves are:

options.text: electromagnetic waves that can travel through vacuum

blocks.explanation: Energy is transferred from the Sun to the Earth by light waves called electromagnetic waves, which can travel through vacuum (7.1).

book_ref.quote: The vast energy of the Sun, millions kilometres away, is transferred to the Earth by light waves.

blocks.prompt: 19 When two waves overlap, their individual displacements are added together to form:

options.text: two separate waves that do not affect each other

blocks.explanation: The resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements, forming a new wave pattern (7.2, Fig. 7.4).

book_ref.quote: then the resultant displacement of the particle is the algebraic sum of their individual displacements

blocks.prompt: 20 Two overlapping waves of displacements 3 cm and 3 cm are in the same phase. The resultant displacement is:
blocks.explanation: In the same phase y = y₁ + y₂; with y₁ = y₂, y = 2y₁ = 2 × 3 = 6 cm (7.2).

book_ref.quote: (i) If two waves, which overlap each other, have same phase

blocks.prompt: 21 Two waves of displacements 5 mm and 2 mm cross each other in opposite phase. The resultant displacement is:
blocks.explanation: In opposite phase y = y₁ − y₂ = 5 − 2 = 3 mm (7.2).

book_ref.quote: (ii) If two waves, which cross each other, have opposite phase

blocks.prompt: 22 Two identical waves of equal displacement meet in opposite phase. The resultant displacement is:
blocks.explanation: In opposite phase y = y₁ − y₂; if y₁ = y₂, then y = 0 (7.2).

book_ref.quote: Particularly, if y₁ = y₂, then resultant displacement will be y = 0.

blocks.prompt: 23 Three waves produce displacements of +4 mm, +3 mm and −5 mm at a particle at the same instant. The resultant displacement is:
blocks.explanation: y = y₁ + y₂ + y₃ = 4 + 3 + (−5) = +2 mm; the displacements are added algebraically (7.2).

book_ref.quote: the resultant displacement y of the particle, under the simultaneous action of these n waves

blocks.prompt: 24 In y(x,t) = y₁(x,t) + y₂(x,t) + … + yₙ(x,t), the function y(x,t) represents the:

options.text: intensity of the wave at x
resultant wave displacement at point x and time t
speed of the wave at time t

blocks.explanation: y(x,t) is the resultant wave function or displacement at point x and time t; it describes the shape of the wave and its evolution (7.2).

book_ref.quote: It describes the shape of the wave and its evolution over time.

blocks.prompt: 25 The principle of superposition applies to:

options.text: linear waves, i.e. waves of small amplitude
only waves of very large amplitude

blocks.explanation: The principle of superposition applies to linear waves, that is, waves of small amplitude (7.2).

book_ref.quote: The principle of superposition applies to linear waves or small

blocks.prompt: 26 Superposition of two waves of slightly different frequencies travelling in the same direction gives:
blocks.explanation: Two waves of slightly different frequencies travelling in the same direction give beats (7.2).

book_ref.quote: Two waves of slightly different frequencies and travelling in the same direction (Beats).

blocks.prompt: 27 Two waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite directions superpose to produce:
blocks.explanation: Two waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite direction produce stationary waves (7.2).

book_ref.quote: Two waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite direction (Stationary waves).

blocks.prompt: 28 In noise-cancelling headphones, the processing unit generates an anti-noise signal which is:

options.text: identical in phase to the ambient noise
exactly opposite to the ambient noise in amplitude and phase
of much higher frequency than the noise
a louder copy of the music

blocks.explanation: The anti-noise signal is the exact opposite of the ambient noise in amplitude and phase, so the two cancel by superposition.

book_ref.quote: which is the exact opposite of the ambient noise (in terms of amplitude and phase)

blocks.prompt: 29 In noise-cancelling headphones, the ambient noise is first captured by:
blocks.explanation: The headphones contain one or more microphones that capture ambient noise; the signals then go to an amplifier and processing unit.

book_ref.quote: The headphones contain one or more microphones that capture ambient noise

blocks.prompt: 30 Superposition of two waves of the same frequency travelling in the same direction is called:
blocks.explanation: Superposition of two waves having the same frequency and travelling in the same direction results in interference (7.3).

book_ref.quote: Superposition of two waves having the same frequency and travelling in the same direction

blocks.prompt: 31 In the interference experiment, the two loudspeakers vibrate in phase because they:

options.text: are driven from the same audio generator

blocks.explanation: Both speakers are driven from the same Audio Generator, so they vibrate in phase; such sources are coherent (7.3).

book_ref.quote: Since the two speakers are driven from the same generator, therefore, they vibrate in phase.

blocks.prompt: 32 In the interference experiment for sound, the CRO is used to:

options.text: display the input signal as a waveform

blocks.explanation: The CRO displays the input signal from the microphone as a waveform on its screen (7.3).

book_ref.quote: The CRO is a device to display the input signal into waveform on its screen.

blocks.prompt: 33 At a point of constructive interference of two sound waves:

options.text: the path difference is half a wavelength

blocks.explanation: At P₁, P₃ and P₅ a compression meets a compression and a rarefaction meets a rarefaction, giving a large displacement (7.3).

book_ref.quote: a compression meets a compression and a rarefaction meets a rarefaction

blocks.prompt: 34 The condition for constructive interference is that the path difference ΔS equals:
blocks.explanation: When the path difference is an integral multiple of wavelength, ΔS = nλ, the waves add up (7.3).

book_ref.quote: Whenever the path difference is an integral multiple of wavelength

blocks.prompt: 35 For destructive interference, the path difference must be:

options.text: an odd integral multiple of λ/2

blocks.explanation: At points of cancellation the path difference is an odd integral multiple of half the wavelength: ΔS = (2n + 1)λ/2 (7.3).

book_ref.quote: the path difference is an odd integral multiple of half the wavelength

blocks.prompt: 36 Two coherent sources of wavelength 0.40 m give a path difference of 1.0 m at a point. At that point there is:

options.text: a node of a stationary wave only

blocks.explanation: 1.0 m = 2.5 λ = (2 × 2 + 1)λ/2, an odd multiple of λ/2, so destructive interference occurs (7.3).

book_ref.quote: At points P₂ and P₄, a compression meets a rarefaction

blocks.prompt: 37 Two coherent sources emit sound of wavelength 0.25 m. At a point the path difference is 0.75 m. The result there is:
blocks.explanation: 0.75 m = 3 × 0.25 m = 3λ, an integral multiple of λ, so constructive interference (7.3).

book_ref.quote: Similarly, at points P₃ and P₅, path difference is zero and −λ, respectively.

blocks.prompt: 38 Two speakers 0.90 m apart emit the same tone of 1100 Hz. A microphone 1.20 m in front of one speaker (opposite it) is at the first point of maximum loudness beside the centre. The speed of sound is:

book_ref.quote: Distance between speakers S₁S₂ = 3.0 m Tone frequency f = 344 Hz

blocks.prompt: 39 A radio transmitter works at 1.5 MHz. Radio waves travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The wavelength is:
blocks.explanation: λ = v/f = 3.0 × 10⁸ / 1.5 × 10⁶ = 200 m (v = fλ, as in Example 7.2).

book_ref.quote: Since, the speed of both the signals is same

blocks.prompt: 40 Sodium chloride in a flame gives out:

options.text: a mixture of red and green light

blocks.explanation: The box says sodium chloride in a flame gives out pure yellow (monochromatic) light, not a mixture of red and green.

book_ref.quote: Monochromatic Light Sodium chloride in a flame gives out pure yellow light.

blocks.prompt: 41 Stationary waves are formed by the superposition of two waves having:

options.text: same frequency and amplitude, travelling in opposite directions
same frequency, travelling in the same direction

blocks.explanation: Stationary waves are formed by two waves with the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions (7.4).

book_ref.quote: They are formed by the superposition of two waves with the same frequency and amplitude, travelling in opposite directions.

blocks.prompt: 42 In a stationary wave, the positions of the nodes and antinodes:

options.text: move forward with the wave speed
move backward with the wave speed

blocks.explanation: The pattern remains stationary, with nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum amplitude) at fixed positions (7.4).

book_ref.quote: with nodes (points of zero amplitude) and antinodes (points of maximum amplitude) at fixed positions

blocks.prompt: 43 A stationary wave has a wavelength of 0.80 m. The distance between two consecutive nodes is:
blocks.explanation: Distance between consecutive nodes = λ/2 = 0.80/2 = 0.40 m (7.4).

book_ref.quote: Here, the distance between two consecutive nodes is λ/2.

blocks.prompt: 44 For a stationary wave of wavelength 0.80 m, the distance between a node and the next antinode is:
blocks.explanation: Node to next antinode = λ/4 = 0.80/4 = 0.20 m (7.4).

book_ref.quote: The distance between a node and the next antinode is λ/4.

blocks.prompt: 45 Two waves, each of amplitude 2 cm, form a stationary wave. The amplitude at an antinode is:
blocks.explanation: Antinodes move with an amplitude equal to the sum of the amplitudes of the component waves: 2 + 2 = 4 cm (7.4).

book_ref.quote: these points are moving with an amplitude which is the sum of the amplitudes of the component waves

blocks.prompt: 46 In a stationary wave, energy does not flow along the medium because:

options.text: the nodes always remain at rest

blocks.explanation: The nodes always remain at rest, so energy cannot flow past them; it remains 'standing' between nodes (7.4).

book_ref.quote: The nodes always remain at rest, so energy cannot flow past these points.

blocks.prompt: 47 When all antinodes of a stationary wave are at their extreme displacements, the energy is:
blocks.explanation: At extreme displacements the energy is wholly potential; passing through equilibrium it is wholly kinetic (7.4).

book_ref.quote: When the antinodes are all at their extreme displacements, the energy stored is wholly potential

blocks.prompt: 48 Which is an example of a stationary wave given in the chapter?

options.text: Sound of a moving train horn

blocks.explanation: Examples of stationary waves include waves on a string and sound waves in a pipe (7.4).

book_ref.quote: The term "standing wave" describes that the wave pattern remains fixed in space

blocks.text: 7.5 Stationary waves on a stretched string

blocks.prompt: 49 A string clamped at both ends is plucked at its middle point. It vibrates with:

options.text: antinodes at both ends and one node in between
nodes at both ends and one antinode in between (one loop)

blocks.explanation: The clamped ends are nodes, with one antinode in between; the string seems to vibrate in one loop (7.5 a).

book_ref.quote: So, nodes will be formed at the two ends and one mode of vibration

blocks.prompt: 50 In the first mode of vibration of a string of length l, the wavelength is:
blocks.explanation: Distance between two consecutive nodes is λ/2, so l = λ₁/2, i.e. λ₁ = 2l (Eq. 7.2).

book_ref.quote: so in this mode of vibration, the length l of the string is

blocks.prompt: 51 The speed of waves on a stretched string depends upon:

options.text: tension and mass per unit length of the string
the point where the string is plucked

blocks.explanation: v = √(F/m) depends on tension F and mass per unit length m; it is independent of the point where the string is plucked (Eq. 7.3).

book_ref.quote: It is independent of the point from where string is plucked to generate wave.

blocks.prompt: 52 A string has a tension of 100 N and mass per unit length 0.04 kg m⁻¹. The speed of transverse waves on it is:

book_ref.quote: The speed v of the waves in the string depends upon the tension F

blocks.prompt: 53 A string 0.50 m long carries waves at 50 m s⁻¹ and vibrates in one loop. Its frequency is:

book_ref.quote: Knowing the speed v and wavelength λ₁, the frequency f₁ of the waves is

blocks.prompt: 54 If the tension in a string is made four times while its length and mass per unit length stay the same, its fundamental frequency:
blocks.explanation: f₁ = (1/2l)√(F/m); f₁ ∝ √F, so four times the tension gives √4 = 2 times the frequency (Eq. 7.4).

book_ref.quote: Thus, in the first mode of vibration shown in Fig. 7.7 (a)

blocks.prompt: 55 When the same string is plucked at one quarter of its length, it vibrates in:
blocks.explanation: Plucked at quarter length (an antinode position), the string vibrates in two loops (7.5 b).

book_ref.quote: Note that now the string vibrates in two loops.

blocks.prompt: 56 In the second mode of vibration of a stretched string of length l:
blocks.explanation: Two loops make l = λ₂, and f₂ = v/l = 2(v/2l) = 2f₁ (7.5 b).

book_ref.quote: so the length l of string is equal to the wavelength of the waves set up in this mode

blocks.prompt: 57 A string vibrating in 4 loops has:
blocks.explanation: With n loops there are (n + 1) nodes and n antinodes: 5 nodes and 4 antinodes (7.5 c).

book_ref.quote: Let the string resonates in n number of loops with (n + 1) nodes and n antinodes.

blocks.prompt: 58 A string 0.90 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrates in 3 loops. The wavelength is:

book_ref.quote: and the corresponding wavelength is,

blocks.prompt: 59 As a stretched string vibrates in more loops, its frequency increases and its wavelength decreases, while:

options.text: their product fλ stays equal to the wave speed v

blocks.explanation: The product of frequency and wavelength is always equal to v, the speed of the waves (7.5 c).

book_ref.quote: However, the product of the frequency f and wavelength λ is always equal to v

blocks.prompt: 60 The existence of only a discrete set of frequencies fₙ = nf₁ on a string is called:
blocks.explanation: Quantum jumps in frequency between resonance frequencies is called quantization of frequencies (7.5 c).

book_ref.quote: This phenomenon is known as the Quantization of Frequencies.

blocks.prompt: 61 On a stretched string, waves whose frequencies are not in the harmonic series:
blocks.explanation: Stationary waves are set up only with frequencies of the harmonic series; others are quickly damped out (7.5 c).

book_ref.quote: Waves which are not in harmonic series are quickly damped out.

blocks.prompt: 62 Once a guitar is tuned, the musician changes the frequency of a string by:

options.text: moving fingers along the neck to change the vibrating length
changing the mass of the string
changing the speed of sound in air

blocks.explanation: Pegs vary the tension; once tuned, musicians move their fingers along the neck, changing the length of the vibrating portion (7.5 c).

book_ref.quote: the tension in guitar and violin strings is varied by tightening the pegs

blocks.prompt: 63 The fundamental frequency of a string is 60 Hz. The frequency of its third harmonic is:
blocks.explanation: fₙ = nf₁, so f₃ = 3 × 60 = 180 Hz; the fundamental is the first harmonic (7.5).

book_ref.quote: The lowest or fundamental frequency of all the harmonics is called the fundamental or first harmonic.

blocks.prompt: 64 A string 1.0 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrates in five segments at 250 Hz. Its fundamental frequency is:
blocks.explanation: fₙ = nf₁ → 250 = 5f₁ → f₁ = 50 Hz (as in Example 7.3).

book_ref.quote: A stationary wave is established in a string which is 120 cm long

blocks.prompt: 65 For the same string (1.0 m long, five segments), the wavelength of the stationary wave is:

book_ref.quote: Subsequent frequencies are called as second harmonic, third harmonic, etc.

blocks.prompt: 66 In an organ pipe, sound is produced due to:

options.text: stationary waves set up in the air column

blocks.explanation: An organ pipe is a wind instrument in which sound is produced by stationary waves in the air column (7.6).

book_ref.quote: An organ pipe is a wind instrument in which sound is produced

blocks.prompt: 67 The open end of an organ pipe behaves as:
blocks.explanation: At an open end the air molecules have complete freedom of motion, so it behaves as an antinode (7.6).

book_ref.quote: (i) If the reflecting end is open, the air molecules have complete freedom of motion

blocks.prompt: 68 The closed end of an organ pipe behaves as a node because:

options.text: the air molecules move freely there
the movement of the air molecules is restricted there

blocks.explanation: A closed reflecting end behaves as a node because the movement of the molecules is restricted (7.6).

book_ref.quote: (ii) If the reflecting end is closed, then it behaves as a node

blocks.prompt: 69 In Fig. 7.8 the waves inside the pipe are drawn as transverse curves, but the actual waves in the air column are:
blocks.explanation: Longitudinal waves set up inside the pipe are represented by transverse curved lines showing displacement and amplitude (7.6).

book_ref.quote: longitudinal waves set up inside the pipe have been represented by transverse curved lines

blocks.prompt: 70 In the fundamental mode of a pipe open at both ends, there are:

options.text: nodes at both ends and one antinode at the middle
one node at the middle and antinodes at both ends

blocks.explanation: There is only one node N at the middle and two antinodes at the open ends, so l = λ₁/2 (7.6).

book_ref.quote: there is only one node N at the middle of the pipe

blocks.prompt: 71 An organ pipe 0.50 m long is open at both ends. Speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Its fundamental frequency is:

book_ref.quote: This frequency is called fundamental frequency or first harmonic.

blocks.prompt: 72 In the second mode of vibration of a pipe open at both ends, there are:
blocks.explanation: The second mode has three antinodes and two nodes, and its frequency is 2f₁ (7.6).

book_ref.quote: If there are three antinodes and two nodes, frequency will be twice that of fundamental frequency.

blocks.prompt: 73 A pipe open at both ends can produce:
blocks.explanation: For an open pipe fₙ = nf₁ with n = 1, 2, 3, …: the whole harmonic series (7.6).

book_ref.quote: So, the longitudinal stationary waves have a discrete set of frequencies

blocks.prompt: 74 A pipe closed at one end is 0.25 m long. The wavelength of its fundamental mode is:
blocks.explanation: One node and one antinode give l = λ₁/4, so λ₁ = 4l = 4 × 0.25 = 1.0 m (Eq. 7.10).

book_ref.quote: Fundamental mode of vibration has one node and one antinode

blocks.prompt: 75 An organ pipe 0.50 m long is closed at one end. Speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Its fundamental frequency is:

book_ref.quote: Let us consider an organ pipe of length l which is closed at one end.

blocks.prompt: 76 The second mode of vibration of a pipe closed at one end has frequency 3f₁. It is the:
blocks.explanation: The harmonic number is f/f₁ = 3, so it is the third harmonic; a closed pipe has only odd harmonics (7.6, book correction).

book_ref.quote: f₃ = 3f₁ is the third harmonic, since the harmonic number is f/f₁ = 3.

blocks.prompt: 77 A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 200 Hz. The next higher frequency it can produce is:
blocks.explanation: A closed pipe has only odd harmonics (n = 1, 3, 5, …), so the next is f₃ = 3 × 200 = 600 Hz (Eq. 7.12).

book_ref.quote: By studying both cases, we conclude that the pipe which is open at both ends is richer in harmonics

blocks.prompt: 78 Two pipes have the same length; one is open at both ends and the other closed at one end. The ratio of their fundamental frequencies (open : closed) is:
blocks.explanation: Open: f₁ = v/2l; closed: f₁ = v/4l; ratio (v/2l)/(v/4l) = 2 : 1 (7.6).

book_ref.quote: Open pipes produce all harmonics, while closed pipes produced only odd harmonics.

blocks.prompt: 79 The shortest pipe of an organ, closed at one end, is 40 mm long. With speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹, its fundamental frequency is:
blocks.explanation: f₁ = v/4l = 340/(4 × 0.040) = 2125 Hz; the shortest pipe gives the highest fundamental (as in Example 7.5).

book_ref.quote: A church organ consists of pipes, each open at one end, of different lengths.

blocks.prompt: 80 In an organ pipe, the steady oscillation is maintained mainly by:

options.text: a wavering sheet-like jet of air from the slit

blocks.explanation: The primary driving mechanism is a wavering, sheet-like jet of air that interacts with the upper lip and the air column (A Scientific Fact).

book_ref.quote: the primary driving mechanism is wavering, sheet like jet of air from flute-slit

blocks.text: 7.7 Experiment demonstrating stationary waves using microwaves

blocks.prompt: 81 Microwaves are called "micro" waves because their wavelengths are of the order of:
blocks.explanation: Their wavelengths are typically millimetres or centimetres, much shorter than radiowaves (7.7).

book_ref.quote: because their wavelengths are typically of the order of millimetres or centimetres

blocks.prompt: 82 A standing wave pattern of microwaves in a cavity is formed when:

options.text: the cavity is open on all sides
the microwaves are absorbed by the walls
the frequency is much lower than radiowaves
the microwave frequency matches the resonant frequency of the cavity

blocks.explanation: A standing wave pattern occurs when the microwave frequency matches the resonant frequency of the cavity (7.7).

book_ref.quote: It occurs when the microwave frequency matches the resonant frequency of the cavity.

blocks.prompt: 83 In the microwave stationary wave experiment, the stationary wave is formed by superposition of the incident wave and the wave:

options.text: emitted by a second source of different frequency

blocks.explanation: Waves from the source are reflected by the metal plate; the reflected and incident waves superpose to make a stationary wave (7.7).

book_ref.quote: The reflected wave and incident wave superpose and create a stationary wave pattern.

blocks.prompt: 84 In a microwave experiment, the probe detector finds adjacent antinodes 1.5 cm apart. The wavelength of the microwaves is:
blocks.explanation: Antinodes are λ/2 apart (7.4), so λ = 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 cm (7.7).

book_ref.quote: By finding the distance from one antinode to the next antinode

blocks.prompt: 85 The apparatus for showing stationary microwaves consists of:

options.text: a ripple tank and a vibrator
a microwave transmitter, a probe detector and a metal reflector in line

blocks.explanation: The setup has a microwave source (transmitter), a probe detector and a metal reflector placed in line (7.7).

book_ref.quote: The experiment setup consists of a microwave source (transmitter), a probe detector and a metal reflector

blocks.prompt: 86 Diffraction can be observed in:

options.text: water, sound, light and other electromagnetic waves

blocks.explanation: Diffraction, the bending of waves around edges, is observed in water, sound, light and electromagnetic waves (7.8).

book_ref.quote: Diffraction can be observed in various types of waves

blocks.prompt: 87 Diffraction is significant when the opening or barrier is:

options.text: comparable in size to the wavelength

blocks.explanation: Diffraction occurs when a wave meets an opening or barrier comparable in size to its wavelength (7.8).

book_ref.quote: that is comparable in size to the wavelength of the wave

blocks.prompt: 88 Waves of wavelengths 1 cm and 3 cm pass through the same gap. Which spreads more?
blocks.explanation: The longer the wavelength, the greater the spreading (7.8).

book_ref.quote: The longer the wavelength, the greater the spreading and vice versa.

blocks.prompt: 89 X-rays are diffracted by crystals because:

options.text: the spacing between atoms is of the order of the X-ray wavelength
atoms in crystals are far apart compared with X-ray wavelength

blocks.explanation: The spacing between regular arrays of atoms is of the order of the X-ray wavelength (7.8).

book_ref.quote: Diffraction of X-rays by crystals as the spacing between the regular arrays of atoms

blocks.prompt: 90 We can hear a person talking around a corner. This is due to:
blocks.explanation: Hearing sound around corners or through a door way is an example of diffraction (7.8).

book_ref.quote: Hearing of sound waves around corners or through door way

blocks.prompt: 91 A ripple tank is used to generate water waves and to demonstrate:
blocks.explanation: A ripple tank generates water waves and demonstrates wave properties such as reflection, diffraction and refraction (7.8).

book_ref.quote: but also to demonstrate wave properties (such as reflection, diffraction and refraction)

blocks.prompt: 92 In a ripple tank, when the gap width is small compared to the wavelength:

options.text: the waves pass straight with no bending
